text: The provided passages list specific areas where AI systems are considered high-risk under Article 6(2) [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. These areas include migration, asylum and border control management [1], and law enforcement in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law [2, 3, 4, 5]. For example, high-risk AI systems in law enforcement can be those intended to be used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities to assess the risk of a natural person becoming the victim of criminal offences [2], or to evaluate the reliability of evidence in the course of the investigation or prosecution of criminal offences [4].

A "serious incident" means an incident or malfunctioning of an AI system that directly or indirectly leads to any of the following [1]: (a) the death of a person, or serious harm to a person’s health; (b) a serious and irreversible disruption of the management or operation of critical infrastructure; (c) the infringement of obligations under Union law intended to protect fundamental rights; or (d) serious harm to property or the environment [1].

A general-purpose AI model is defined as an AI model that displays significant generality and is capable of competently performing a wide range of distinct tasks regardless of how it is placed on the market and can be integrated into various downstream systems or applications [1](63). This definition includes AI models that are trained with a large amount of data using self-supervision at scale, provided they are not used for research, development, or prototyping activities before being placed on the market [1](63).

This Regulation does not apply to obligations of deployers who are natural persons using AI systems in the course of a purely personal non-professional activity [1]. Therefore, the deployer obligations do not apply to you if you use an AI app at home for a personal hobby [1].

Yes, the rules cover testing and development of an AI system before it is put on the market. Article 1 states that the Regulation does not apply to research, testing, or development activity regarding AI systems or AI models prior to their being placed on the market or put into service, provided such activities are conducted in accordance with applicable Union law [1]. Furthermore, the testing of high-risk AI systems must be performed, as appropriate, at any time throughout the development process and in any event prior to their being placed on the market or put into service, using prior defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds [2].

Data governance practices for training, validation, and testing data sets must cover several aspects [1]. These practices concern design choices, data collection processes and the origin of data, and the original purpose of personal data collection [1]. They also involve relevant data-preparation processing operations such as annotation, labelling, cleaning, updating, enrichment, and aggregation [1]. Furthermore, they require the formulation of assumptions about the information the data is supposed to measure and represent [1]. An assessment of the availability, quantity, and suitability of the data sets is also required [1].

Yes, high-risk AI systems must technically allow for the automatic recording of events, which are logs, over the system's lifetime [13(1)]. These logs must record events relevant to identifying situations that may result in the high-risk AI system presenting a risk or a substantial modification, facilitating post-market monitoring, and monitoring the operation of the system [13(2)]. Providers of high-risk AI systems are required to keep the logs automatically generated by their high-risk AI systems to the extent they are under their control [19(e)].

Yes, providers established in third countries must appoint an authorised representative established in the Union before making their high-risk AI systems available on the Union market [3]. This is required by a written mandate [3].

Yes, providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems may exceptionally process special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction [1][2][3][4][5]. This processing is allowed to the extent that it is strictly necessary to ensure bias detection and correction in relation to high-risk AI systems as per Article 10(2), points (f) and (g) [2][3][4][5]. This processing is subject to appropriate safeguards for the fundamental rights and freedoms of natural persons [2][3][4][5].

Article 5, point 1(ba), prohibits the placing on the market, putting into service, or use of an AI system that generates or manipulates realistic images, videos, audio, or similar material of an identifiable natural person's intimate parts, or of an identifiable natural person engaged in sexually explicit activities, without that person's freely-given, specific, informed, unambiguous, and explicit consent for that generation or manipulation [1]. However, an AI system that manipulates material in a way that does not increase the exposure of any depicted intimate parts or alter the nature of any depicted sexually explicit activities shall not constitute manipulation [2].

No, the placing on the market, putting into service for a specific purpose, or using an AI system for making risk assessments of natural persons to assess or predict the risk of a natural person committing a criminal offence based solely on the profiling of a natural person or on assessing their personality traits and characteristics is prohibited [1][4]. This prohibition does not apply to AI systems used to support the human assessment of the involvement of a person in a criminal activity, which is already based on objective and verifiable facts directly linked to a criminal activity [1].

Yes, the placing on the market, putting into service for a specific purpose, or the use of biometric categorisation systems that categorize individuals based on their biometric data to deduce or infer their religious or philosophical beliefs is prohibited [1(g)].

Yes, an AI tool that screens and filters job applications can be high-risk. This is because AI systems intended to be used for the recruitment or selection of natural persons, which includes placing targeted job advertisements, analyzing and filtering job applications, and evaluating candidates, are listed as high-risk systems [1][4].

AI systems intended to establish credit scores for natural persons are considered high-risk, with an exception for AI systems used for the purpose of detecting financial fraud [1][2]. The list of high-risk AI systems includes AI systems intended to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or establish their credit score, with the exception of AI systems used for the purpose of detecting financial fraud [1].

No, AI systems that are solely used for non-safety related aspects such as convenience or performance optimisation shall not qualify as safety components [1a]. However, an AI system can qualify as a safety component if its failure or malfunctioning would endanger health and safety [2].

Yes, AI systems intended to be used as safety components in the management and operation of critical digital infrastructure, such as the supply of water or electricity, are considered high-risk AI systems [1][2]. This is because they are listed in the areas referred to in Article 6(2) [1].

The reporting timeline for a serious incident depends on the circumstances. If the death of a person is involved, the report must be provided immediately after the provider or deployer establishes, or as soon as it suspects, a causal relationship between the high-risk AI system and the serious incident, but not later than 10 days after the provider or, where applicable, the deployer becomes aware of the serious incident [1]. For other serious incidents, the report must be made immediately after the provider has established a causal link or the reasonable likelihood of such a link, and in any event, not later than 15 days after the provider or, where applicable, the deployer, becomes aware of the serious incident, taking into account the severity of the incident [5].

Providers of AI systems that generate synthetic audio, image, video, or text content must ensure that the outputs of the AI system are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated [1][2]. Deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates image, audio, or video content constituting a deep fake shall disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated [3][4]. This obligation does not apply if the use is authorized by law to detect, prevent, investigate, or prosecute a criminal offence [3].

Providers must ensure that natural persons are informed that they are interacting with an AI system unless it is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant, and circumspect person considering the circumstances and context [1]. This information must be provided to the concerned natural persons in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure [2].

Providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, generating synthetic audio, image, video or text content, that have been placed on the market before 2 August 2026 must take the necessary steps to comply with Article 50(2) by 2 December 2026 [4].

A general-purpose AI model is presumed to have high impact capabilities if the cumulative amount of computation used for its training, measured in floating point operations, is greater than $10^{25}$ [1][2].

Providers of general-purpose AI models must draw up and keep up-to-date the technical documentation of the model, which includes its training and testing process and the results of its evaluation [1]. This technical documentation must contain at least the information set out in Annex XI [1]. Annex XI specifies the information that must be provided, which includes a general description of the model, a detailed description of its elements and development process, and technical means required for integration [3][4][5].

Providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk must perform model evaluation using standardized protocols and tools, which includes conducting and documenting adversarial testing to identify and mitigate systemic risks [1][1(a)]. They must also assess and mitigate possible systemic risks at the Union level, including their sources, that may arise from the development, market placement, or use of such models [1][1(b)]. Furthermore, they are required to keep track of, document, and report, without undue delay, relevant information about serious incidents and possible corrective measures to the AI Office and, as appropriate, to national competent authorities [1][1(c)]. They must also ensure an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for the general-purpose AI model with systemic risk and its physical infrastructure [1][1(d)].

Providers of general-purpose AI models that have been placed on the market before 2 August 2025 must take the necessary steps to comply with the obligations laid down in this Regulation by 2 August 2027 [1].

The maximum administrative fine for non-compliance with the prohibition of AI practices referred to in Article 5 is EUR 35,000,000 or up to 7% of the undertaking's total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher [1]. For non-compliance with the prohibition of AI practices, administrative fines on Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies are up to EUR 1,500,000 [2]. Furthermore, non-compliance with any requirements or obligations under this Regulation, other than those laid down in Article 5, is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 750,000 [5].

The supply of incorrect, incomplete, or misleading information to notified bodies or national competent authorities in reply to a request is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 7,500,000 or up to 1% of the undertaking's total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher [1]. Additionally, the Commission may impose fines not exceeding 3% of the provider's annual total worldwide turnover or EUR 15,000,000, whichever is higher, if the provider intentionally or negligently supplies incorrect, incomplete, or misleading information [2].

Authorities consider all relevant circumstances of the specific situation when deciding on the amount of an administrative fine in each individual case [1][2][3][4][5]. Specifically, they shall regard factors such as any other aggravating or mitigating factor applicable to the circumstances, like financial benefits gained or losses avoided [1(e)], the degree of cooperation with national competent authorities [2(f)], whether administrative fines have already been applied by other market surveillance authorities for the same infringement [3(b)], the size, annual turnover, and market share of the operator committing the infringement [4(d)], and whether administrative fines have already been applied by other authorities to the same operator for infringements of other Union or national law resulting from the same activity or omission [5(c)].

The Commission may impose fines not exceeding 3% of the provider's annual total worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year or EUR 15,000,000, whichever is higher [1]. The amount of the fine will be determined by considering the nature, gravity, and duration of the infringement, taking into account the principles of proportionality and appropriateness [1].

Downstream providers have the right to lodge a complaint alleging an infringement of this Regulation [2]. A complaint must be duly reasoned and include the point of contact of the provider, a description of the relevant facts and provisions, and any other relevant information [2][2].

Deployers of high-risk AI systems must keep the logs automatically generated by that system for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system, of at least six months, unless otherwise required by applicable Union or national law [1]. Providers of high-risk AI systems shall keep the logs referred to in Article 12(1), automatically generated by their high-risk AI systems, for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system, of at least six months, unless provided otherwise in the applicable Union or national law, particularly in Union law on the protection of personal data [2].

The provided passages do not specify which particular chatbots or AI models the Commission has designated as having systemic risk. The passages describe the criteria for designating general-purpose AI models with systemic risk and the procedure for reassessing such designations [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].
